title: CVE-2026-84170 - Apache Wicket: Configured upload limits are not enforced by the standalone file upload resource
text:
8.3

HIGH
CVSS 4.0

CVE-2026-84170
Apache Wicket: Configured upload limits are not enforced by the standalone file upload resource

Allocation of resources without limits or throttling in Apache Wicket.

org.apache.wicket.markup.html.form.upload.resource.AbstractFileUploadResource is the server side of the form-less upload offered by FileUploadToResourceField, which posts the selected files to a separately mounted resource rather than through a Form. The resource is an application-wide singleton with no component to consult, so newResourceResponse() takes the three limits that bound the upload - the total request size, the maximum size of a single part and the maximum number of parts - from the request parameters maxSize, fileMaxSize and fileCountMax, and hands them to the multipart parser as they arrive. Nothing binds those numbers to the field that is supposed to be uploading. A request naming a very large maxSize is therefore parsed with no effective ceiling on the total size, and omitting fileMaxSize and fileCountMax leaves the per-part and part-count limits unset as well. The values the application configured through FileUploadToResourceField#setMaxSize(), #setFileMaxSize() and #setFileCountMax() are consulted only when the client omits the corresponding parameter, so against a client that supplies one they have no effect at all.

Parts above the parser's in-memory threshold are spooled to the container's temporary directory, and the file parts are then copied into the folder the application's IUploadsFileManager owns, under a sub-folder the request names, where they remain. A part that is not a file is read into the heap in full while the request is parsed. One request, repeatable, can therefore consume as much disk or as much heap as the client chooses to send. The resource carries no authorization annotation and the default authorization strategy permits every resource request, so unless the application authorizes the resource itself the request needs no authentication, no session, no prior page view and no user interaction.

An application is affected where it uses FileUploadToResourceField, or mounts FileUploadResourceReference itself. This is not the ordinary upload path: the resource is a singleton that has to be created and mounted deliberately. An application that configures no upload limit at all loses nothing, because Wicket applies no total-size limit of its own by default; what the defect removes is a limit the application set. Uploads through Form with FileUploadField, and through AjaxFileDropBehavior, are not affected, because both read their limits from the component rather than from the request. The upload resource does not exist in the 8.x line.

This issue affects Apache Wicket: from 9.14.0 through 9.24.0, from 10.0.0 through 10.9.1. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 9.25.0 or 10.12.0, which fix the issue.

title: CVE-2026-83594 - Apache Wicket: FileUploadToResourceField accepts a client-asserted upload result and allocates the size it names
text:
8.3

HIGH
CVSS 4.0

CVE-2026-83594
Apache Wicket: FileUploadToResourceField accepts a client-asserted upload result and allocates the size it names

Memory allocation with an excessive size value in Apache Wicket.

org.apache.wicket.markup.html.form.upload.resource.FileUploadToResourceField uploads files to a separately mounted resource rather than through a form, and is told the outcome afterwards over its own Ajax callback. That callback reads the request parameter filesInfo, a JSON array carrying a client file name, a size and a content type for each file, and turns it into the list of FileUploadToResourceField.UploadInfo that onUploadSuccess() receives. Nothing binds that JSON to an upload the resource performed and nothing re-derives it from the stored files, so the number of entries and every value in them are whatever the request supplied. The callback URL is rendered into the page, no prior upload is required, and both GET and POST reach it, so any client that can load the page can have the component report files that were never uploaded, without authenticating beyond whatever the page itself requires and without any user interaction.

UploadInfo#get(), which the class offers as the way to obtain the bytes of an upload, allocates a byte array from UploadInfo#getSize() before it opens the file. The array is therefore sized by the number the request supplied, and the allocation happens even for a file that was never stored. One small request can cost the server close to two gigabytes of heap, and the request is trivially repeatable, so a few of them exhaust the heap for every request the Java virtual machine is serving. A size that the conversion to int turns negative instead throws NegativeArraySizeException, which the exception handler inside that method does not cover, so it escapes into the application.

An application is affected where it uses FileUploadToResourceField, which is not the ordinary upload path through FileUploadField and Form and has to be extended and mounted deliberately. The allocation additionally requires the application to call UploadInfo#get() rather than reading UploadInfo#getFile() itself. Where the application denies the ENABLE action on the field through its authorization strategy, the callback is refused like any other listener. The 8.x line does not contain this component and is not affected.

This issue affects Apache Wicket: from 9.14.0 through 9.24.0, from 10.0.0 through 10.11.0. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 9.25.0 or 10.12.0, which fix the issue.

CVE-2026-120308
Beta9 host filesystem exposure via volume path traversal

A Beta9 tenant can attach a volume when deploying a function, endpoint, or task queue. The gateway builds the host path by joining the shared volumes root, the workspace name, and the volume identifier from the stub configuration. Nothing checks that the identifier names a volume that workspace owns. text:
9.9

CRITICAL
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-120307
Beta9 container escape via unvalidated sandbox file paths

The Beta9 worker serves the sandbox file API from outside the container. getHostPathFromContainerPath turns the tenant's container path into a worker path. If the unresolved path starts with a mount destination, including the default upload mount at /tmp/.beta9, the remainder is joined onto that mount's source with filepath.Join, which cleans parent-directory segments after the prefix check. A long enough run of those segments names any absolute path on the worker. A path that matches no mount is joined onto the container root and opened in the worker's own filesystem, so an absolute symbolic link such as /var/run pointing at /run is followed against the worker root. Upload, download, stat, list, find-in-files, replace-in-files, and delete-file all call this helper. A tenant with a workspace token and one running sandbox can read, write, list, and delete files on the hosting worker as root, including files of other tenants on that machine. A read-only proof downloaded the worker pod's Kubernetes service account token through the file API for a path that did not exist inside the sandbox. In the shipped remote-node manifests that service account is bound to cluster-admin. Fixed in worker 0.1.756: sandbox file operations and workspace sync open paths with os.OpenRoot, so parent-directory and symlink lookups stay inside the container root or the mount source.

title: CVE-2026-120306 - Beta9 build sandbox escape via chroot-only isolation
text:
9.9

CRITICAL
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-120306
Beta9 build sandbox escape via chroot-only isolation

Beta9 turns each shell command in a tenant image definition into a Dockerfile RUN line and executes it with Buildah on the build worker. The worker image sets BUILDAH_ISOLATION=chroot, and no buildah invocation passes --isolation, so the step only changes its filesystem root. It keeps the worker pod's PID, network, IPC, and user namespaces, runs as uid 0, and holds CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE. PID 1 in that procfs is the worker entrypoint, so /proc/1/root is the worker container's filesystem and is writable. That filesystem contains the runc, buildah, and runsc binaries the worker uses to start tenant containers, the worker's Kubernetes service account token, and the host directories mounted into the pod. title: CVSS 10.0 LXD, MicroCloud Flaw Lets Attackers Impersonate Trusted Clients Without a Private Key
text:
CVSS 10.0 LXD, MicroCloud Flaw Lets Attackers Impersonate Trusted Clients Without a Private KeySwati KhandelwalNov 01, 2026Vulnerability / Cloud Security

//<![CDATA[
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded",()=>{let t=document.querySelector("h1.story-title"),m=document.querySelector(".postmeta");t&&m&&t.insertAdjacentElement("afterend",m)})
//]]>

A critical flaw in Canonical's LXD and MicroCloud let an attacker log in as a trusted client without holding that client's private key. To do it, the attacker had to reach their HTTPS API over the network and have the trusted client's public certificate.

Once in, the attacker would act as that client, with access to the cluster and its virtual machines. If the impersonated account is privileged, the attacker could gain "root access to the host machine," Canonical said.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-112816, carries a maximum CVSS score of 10.0, and Canonical has released fixed versions of both products.

How the Flaw Works

LXD and MicroCloud let remote clients access their APIs over mutual TLS, a setup in which the client presents a certificate to prove who it is. A client is trusted when its certificate is in the server's trust store, the list of identities the server will accept.

The flaw was in how the server checked that certificate. It compared every certificate the client sent against the trust store, but a TLS connection only proves the client owns the private key for the first certificate in the chain, the leaf. The rest of the chain is whatever the client chose to attach.

So an attacker could take a trusted client's public certificate, which is not secret, attach it to the chain behind their own, and the server would accept them as that client.

Who Is Affected

Using the flaw takes two things: network access to the HTTPS API, and the public certificate of a client the server already trusts.

A standalone LXD server does not expose that API by default. It listens only on a local socket unless an administrator turns on the network API with the core.https_address setting.

MicroCloud, which ties several machines running LXD into one cluster, has a specific weak point. Canonical said an attacker who can capture a member's public certificate as it joins the cluster can then log in as that member.

The CVE record lists LXD 4.0.14, 5.0.10, 5.21.8 and 6.9 as affected, each before the fixed release that follows. Canonical lists these fixed snap versions:

The bug did not start at Canonical. The Incus project, which began as a community fork of LXD, reported it, and Canonical confirmed it affected LXD as well. Incus fixed the same flaw in version 7.6.0.

Ubuntu's own archive packages of LXD are listed as not affected or not shipped, so the fixed releases are the snaps.

There is no public sign the flaw has been used in an attack. The CVE record carries a U.S. CISA assessment, dated October 30, that the flaw is not known to have been exploited; it is not on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list, and no working exploit has been published.

What to Do

Update LXD and MicroCloud to the fixed versions. On a snap install, run sudo snap refresh lxd and sudo snap refresh microcloud.

Canonical said the fixed LXD point releases were still rolling out from the candidate channel to stable at the time of its advisory, so check the version you actually have after the refresh rather than assume the fix arrived.

Canonical's advisory gives no temporary workaround for LXD. Because the attack requires network access to the API, limiting who can reach it reduces risk until you update. The Incus project, reporting the same flaw, said there is no configuration fix and that the only step is to restrict network access to the listener.

SentinelOne Prompt Security: What It Is, and How I Actually Tested It
text: Every company I talk to has the same quiet worry right now: people are pasting things into ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot that should never leave the building. API keys. Customer records. Whole .env files. The AI is useful, so nobody wants to ban it, but nobody can see what is going into it either. That gap is exactly what a product like Prompt Security is supposed to close, and when SentinelOne picked it up it landed on my desk to evaluate properly.So I did what I usually do: I stopped reading the datasheet and spent a few weeks actually running it. Real tenant, real browsers, real coding tools, fake secrets. This series is the write-up of what I found - what it catches, where it is strong, and the places it quietly lets things through. This first part is the setup: what the product is, what I had access to, and the rules I tested it under. If you want the juicy bypasses, they are coming, but you will understand them a lot better once you know how the thing is built. What Prompt Security actually isStrip away the marketing and it is a DLP layer that sits between your people and the AI they use. It reads the prompt on its way out, decides whether it contains something sensitive - a secret, a card number, personal data - and then does something about it: lets it go, redacts the sensitive bit, swaps in dummy data, or blocks the whole thing. The clever part is where it does the reading, because "AI" is not one place. People use it in a browser tab, in a desktop app, and increasingly from the command line. Prompt Security covers those with two separate pieces.The browser extensionThis is the half that watches AI in the browser - chatgpt.com, claude.ai, Gemini, Copilot, Perplexity, and also the AI baked into ordinary sites like Notion, Gmail's "Help me write" and the Edge Copilot sidebar. It is the only piece that can read text inside an uploaded screenshot or a Word file, and it is the piece that shows the user a pop-up when something is blocked.The endpoint agentThis is the half that covers everything that is not a browser tab: the desktop apps (the Claude and ChatGPT installers, Copilot in VS Code) and the coding assistants that talk to a model API directly, including Claude Code and OpenCode pointed at Bedrock. Under the hood it installs a local proxy and its own certificate so it can see inside the encrypted traffic on its way to the model. That is a detail that matters later, so file it away.What was unlocked, and what wasn'tWorth being honest about scope up front, because it shapes everything. The product comes in three modules, and for now I only had the Employees product switched on - the part that governs how staff use AI. The other two, Homegrown Apps (for AI you build into your own products) Agentic AI (for autonomous agents), were not avaliable on my license. So for now this whole series is about employee AI use. The other two modules are on my list - I plan to test them and write them up the same way once I can get them unlocked - but everything you read here is the Employees side only.The tenant also started in Monitor mode - watching and logging, blocking nothing - which is the sensible way to start any DLP rollout. Part of the test was walking it from "just watching" through to actually enforcing, and seeing what broke along the way.Employees (AI usage + AI code assistants) - what I tested, and what this series covers.Homegrown Apps - locked for now; to be tested and written up later.Agentic AI discovery - locked for now; to be tested and written up later. How I tested itI did not want a tidy demo. I wanted to know whether a normal person doing normal things - and an annoyed person trying to get around it - would be caught. So I ran the same canary secret through every channel I could get my hands on and logged whether it was detected, what action fired, and how long it took to show up in the console.One thing to be clear about up front: everything in this series so far was tested on Windows. SMS OF DEATH: ANDROID UNDER ATTACK, AN INVISIBLE SMS CAN BLOCK CALLS AND EMERGENCY SERVICES
Pierluigi Paganini

November 01, 2026
SMS of Death lets attackers crash Android call services with a hidden, zero-click message, blocking phone calls, even emergency calls too.

A specially manipulated SMS message is enough to crash Android’s phone service, interrupt ongoing calls, and temporarily render the smartphone unusable. The attack requires no interaction from the victim and can even compromise the ability to contact emergency services.

The vulnerability, dubbed the SMS of Death, is bringing renewed attention to the security of the messaging system in Android smartphones. The issue, documented by independent researcher Mark Blaszczyk, allows a remote attacker to cause a disruption in phone service by sending a single, specially crafted WAP Push message.

WAP Push (Wireless Application Protocol Push) is a particular message transmitted over the mobile network, generally in the form of a binary SMS, which contains structured data and is processed automatically by the smartphone without requiring user intervention. Unlike a traditional SMS, it can carry notifications, links to Internet resources, and configurations for mobile services.

The most worrying aspect is the execution method. It’s a zero-click attack, in which the recipient doesn’t have to open the message, select a link, or authorize any action. The content is automatically processed by the operating system and can cause the process responsible for phone functionality to crash.

The vulnerability affects “WapPushOverSms“, an Android framework component located in the “frameworks/opt/telephony” path, responsible for interpreting and managing WAP Push messages received by the device.

text:
in recent times i've been asked a lot the question of "what ai model did you find to use this?", practically for all of the articles on this blog. the answer has always been my brain, i have never used ai for any kind of research i published, ever.
the next question is often why, followed up with "you would be so unstoppable with claude mythos" this article should explain why i don't like using ai for my research, and my general opinions on llms in both development and cybersecurity
why i don't use ai
it's as simple as i do this for fun, and i don't find giving an ai all the fun at poking at something instead of doing it myself fun. put it another way, i like using my brain
i like coding, i like staring at devtools, binary ninja, or whatever else for hours, i like exploring weird library source code and tracing it with nothing but github code search and a dream, it is fun to me. i don't do anything on this blog for money, i do it for fun, the money part is just a nice side effect
but why don't you just offload the tedious bits to ai?
a lot of the tedious bits are still fun, there's some that aren't, but i also cannot take credit for something an llm did for me, and i am wildly uncomfortable with publishing something an llm did for me on my personal blog as a writeup
this blog is mine, all the work on it is mine, or is shared research with other people that are explicitly credited. i cannot take credit for something an llm did for me, and i also cannot credit an llm properly, as they aren't a person
using an llm makes me lose my mind
i truly have tried to use llms before, just to try it out. nothing i was going to publish as research, but i really couldn't and it left me never wanting to use an llm again
i don't know how more people don't experience this, but staring at an llms output be confidently wrong eventually to get there in the process, or looking at the commands its running and see some really stupid things its doing drives me crazy to the point i will just stop it before it answers, i cannot handle something being that confidently wrong (even though it'll probably still get there in the end)
i'm not denying these models are powerful
llms are quite powerful machines, we've seen that as of recent, that's for sure, they are still wildly marketed as being more powerful then they are, but i cannot argue that they are infact not powerful, because they are
llms still need guidance
if you threw an llm at the linux kernel and told it to find an rce without any other guidance, it probably couldn't. you still need skill and experience to guide an llm at the current state
all of these vulnerabilities that we've been panicking over have been found by skilled researchers using llms, likely at a big firm to give them all the tokens they want. because llms still need guidance and not anyone can just do this, no matter what openai or anthropic try to tell you
marketing and php2shell
ai companies have hooked onto cybersecurity as their marketing strategy and it shows, a good example is php2shell. where three companies:

calif (research firm)
openai (you know who openai is)
wiz (research firm)

all collaborated on it and released their own blogposts, all seemingly with different narratives
calif went with the narrative of an ai found these php vulns with the help of a human guiding it, while openai went with the agent uncovered critical vulnerabilties, and wiz went with a middle point, still pretty openai-like
"patch the world"
openai talked a lot about how they were helping maintainers patch these issues, and mitigate them faster and for more people. which i'm sure they did to an extent, but i don't think they did all they could
they could easily backport these security fixes to older versions of php with the help of ai if they wanted to, it's not like they don't have the compute, they do, they have a lot of it, they're openai
dropping poc videos before patch
this has been a common trend in the recent days of ai-based cybersecurity […]

An investigation by CrowdStrike has uncovered a series of cyberattacks against nine major South Korean banks, attributed to a 26-year-old amateur hacker based in southern China. The attacker leveraged publicly available Artificial Intelligence (AI) chatbots to execute the breaches, leading to the theft and exposure of financial data from tens of thousands of customers. The incident highlights a significant shift in the threat landscape, where AI tools are lowering the barrier to entry for cybercrime, enabling unskilled individuals to conduct effective attacks. The attacker's poor operational security led to their identification, revealing they also used AI to find buyers for the stolen data and to generate a fake cybersecurity résumé.
Threat Overview
Between late 2025 and early 2026, an amateur attacker successfully compromised at least nine financial institutions in South Korea. The primary vector involved the use of AI chatbots to generate malicious code and orchestrate the attacks. Despite the attacker's limited technical expertise, the accessibility of advanced AI models provided the necessary capabilities to breach the banks' defenses. The goal of the operation was financial data theft, which the attacker subsequently attempted to monetize by selling it online. This incident is a practical example of the weaponization of AI, a threat that security experts and government agencies like the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) have been increasingly warning about.
Technical Analysis
The attacker reportedly used AI chatbots to perform several stages of the attack lifecycle. This likely included generating phishing emails, writing exploit code for known vulnerabilities, and creating scripts for data exfiltration. The success of the campaign underscores how AI can automate and simplify complex attack techniques. The investigation by CrowdStrike was aided by significant operational security failures on the part of the attacker, who left behind digital traces linking back to their identity and location.

Impact Assessment
The immediate impact includes the exposure of sensitive financial data for tens of thousands of customers across nine South Korean banks, placing them at high risk of fraud and identity theft. text: Comment13Save StorySave this storyComment13Save StorySave this story from The Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto revealed a worst-case scenario found in the wild: spyware silently infecting targets as they browse past ads in their daily digital lives.Dubbing the attacks “AdFection,” the researchers documented a campaign in which an Israeli-registered advertising firm allegedly connected to the servers linked to a spyware company and infected dozens of devices with its invasive malware. Citizen Lab believes this to be the first detailed technical evidence made publicly available of sophisticated spyware infecting devices via digital ads.Zero-click hacks are a holy grail for attackers and catastrophic for victims, because they can automatically install malware on devices without requiring any interaction or missteps from the target. When sophisticated hackers have deployed rare zero-click attacks in recent years, they have often exploited vulnerabilities in mobile messaging and communication apps to infect victims. But attackers have also exploited the sprawling infrastructure of the online ad ecosystem to distribute malware, sometimes with little or no interaction needed from victims. Evidence of the zero-click spyware campaign that Citizen Lab’s researchers uncovered shows the two threats merging, underscoring the extent and urgency of the risk. Hackers Stalked Me by Hijacking a Smartwatch for Kids“AdFection allows operators to automatically hack specific individuals with mercenary spyware as they use apps or browse the internet,” says Bill Marczak, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab. “Someone who gets hacked like this would not see anything amiss. In fact, they might not even see any ad at all.”The situation is so concerning, he notes, because there isn’t much that people can do to protect themselves from zero-click ad attacks other than blocking ads as thoroughly as possible on all websites and platforms—a fact that intelligence agencies like the NSA and CIA seem to know all too well. “The risk of having your device infected with spyware simply by using a website or app that displays ads is a nightmare scenario,” says Wolfie Christl, a senior Citizen Lab researcher.During 2024 and 2025, Citizen Lab concluded that 45 devices belonging to the news outlet Al Jazeera were targeted with zero-click attacks delivered by ads. The researchers say that the targeted ads were issued by the Israeli-founded marketing firm Discover-Tech and distributed spyware attributed to the Israeli developer Candiru. Infected devices had contact with domains linked to Discover-Tech and then connected to infrastructure associated with Candiru, according to Citizen Lab’s analysis. (Al Jazeera, which participated in the investigation and shared device logs with Citizen Lab researchers, did not respond to a request for comment.) text: Flock keeps ignoring requests to cancel its contractsCities are canceling Flock contracts, but the company won’t take them down and sometimes is reinstalling them.Cities are canceling Flock contracts, but the company won’t take them down and sometimes is reinstalling them.by Nov 1, 2026, 7:58 PM UTC Comments88Comments (All New) Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty ImagesPart OfThe fight over Flock and other ALPRssee all updates Terrence O'Brien is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.While more cities are canceling their contracts with Flock Safety, just as many are discovering how difficult that can be in some instances. Plymouth, Minnesota’s city council voted to terminate its contract with Flock in September, but failed to respond to the city’s request. For over a month, the cameras remained up, and the city had received no acknowledgment from the company. So, Police Chief Eric Fadden took matters into his own hands and physically disconnected the cameras.“After hearing nothing for more than a week, I directed our staff to disconnect the power cords from the cameras in order to be sure that they are not functioning or recording plates,” Fadden told The Drive.Roughly 20 miles up the road, Dayton, Minnesota, is having its own issues with Flock. In this instance, the company acknowledged the city’s request and said it would take up to 60 days to remove the equipment. Despite this, Flock reconnected two cameras within the city limits without authorization, and following a specific request from the local police not to complete the work order. Dayton’s local government posted on Facebook:On September 17, 2026, the Police Department was made aware of a maintenance work order produced by Flock. The City notified Flock on September 18, 2026, that the program was on hold, and no work orders were to be completed. Unfortunately, the City’s direction was not followed, and the camera was placed back into service without authorization.Flock spokesperson Andrew Smith told The Verge, “We are proud of the impact our technology has had in Plymouth. We respect the city’s decision and are working with the customer to have the cameras removed.”This follows a similar ordeal in Illinois, where the company refused to take down cameras and uncovered cameras at Elgin Community College after the administration sought to cancel its contract.Update November 1st: Added comment from Flock.8 CommentsFollow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

CVE-2026-78030 is an unvalidated module-loading flaw in DBI versions before 1.653 for Perl, specifically in the DBD::DBM driver. The vulnerability resides in the DBD::DBM database driver shipped with DBI for Perl. When a caller establishes a connection using a DSN of the form dbi:DBM:..., the driver consumes the dbm_type and dbm_mldbm connect attributes. According to the NVD description, DBI versions before 1.653 pass the values of these two attributes directly to Perl's require without checking that the value actually names a module.
This is dangerous because of how require resolves its argument. As stated in the advisory, require treats a path-shaped string as a literal filename and does not consult @INC. In a widespread campaign dubbed "Black October," security researchers at Wiz have identified a series of targeted attacks against at least nine AI developer platforms. The list of victims includes Northflank, Railway, OpenCode, Warp, Lightning AI, Fireworks AI, Andromeda, Zeabur, and CommandCode. The attackers' primary objective was to steal API keys and other credentials stored as environment variables on these platforms. This stolen access was then used to make unauthorized calls to expensive AI model services, a technique Wiz has named "LLMJacking." The financial impact is substantial, with over $100,000 in fraudulent AI service usage documented. The campaign was sophisticated, with some victims reporting "agent swarm" attacks, and led to severe consequences, including the complete shutdown of the Zeabur platform.
Threat Overview
The attacks, which took place throughout October 2026, represent a systematic assault on the AI development supply chain. Threat actors focused on a common vulnerability point: the storage of sensitive credentials, particularly AI service API keys, within the environment variables of cloud-based development platforms. On October 30, 2026, Northflank publicly disclosed a breach after being alerted by Wiz, confirming that attackers had accessed and abused customer AI API keys. The coordinated nature of the attacks, while not definitively linked to a single threat actor, suggests a shared methodology targeting a specific weakness in the AI ecosystem. The term "LLMJacking" has been coined to describe this new threat pattern of hijacking resources for Large Language Model (LLM) computation, similar to traditional cryptojacking.
Technical Analysis
The core of the attack involved gaining access to the developer platforms and reading environment variables where users stored their credentials for services like OpenAI, Anthropic, or others. The method of initial access to the platforms was not detailed but could range from exploiting platform vulnerabilities to using stolen developer credentials.
Once the API keys were stolen, attackers used them to run their own AI workloads, billing the cost to the legitimate key owners. Several victims, including Fireworks, OpenCode, and Warp, reported signs of an "agent swarm" attack, which may imply the use of multiple autonomous AI agents to carry out tasks, possibly for model training, inference, or further attacks. Other victims noted the activity seemed related to "distillation," a process for training smaller, more efficient AI models by learning from a larger one.
MITRE ATT&CK Techniques

T1552.005 - Cloud Instance Metadata API: While not explicitly stated, accessing environment variables in cloud platforms is analogous to querying metadata services for credentials.
T1528 - Steal Application Access Token: The primary goal was to steal API keys, which are a form of application access token.
T1078 - Valid Accounts: The stolen API keys represent valid accounts for AI services, which the attackers then abused.
T1496 - Resource Hijacking: This is the essence of "LLMJacking"—hijacking computational resources (in this case, expensive AI services) for the attacker's benefit.

Impact Assessment
The "Black October" campaign has had a severe impact on the victims and the broader AI development community. Direct financial losses exceeded $100,000 in fraudulent charges […]

Malaysia Airlines Reports Three-Year Data Exposure via Amadeus System Breach

Attackers gained unauthorized access to the passenger reservation systems used by MAB and several other major Asian carriers.The security incident exposed data from a three-year window from August 2023 to September 2026. # AI Agents Don't Sign NDAs

There are reports going around that a Claude Code agent lived inside a Pentagon network for two months before anyone caught it; accenture says it didn't happen. But usually, when a contractor denies a breach while data is already leaking out, they aren't arguing about the facts, and they're arguing about who has to pay the bill.

This isn't just some basic stolen password. The real horror here is the dwell time and who was actually doing the work. Imagine being a SOC lead and finding out an autonomous agent stayed hidden for two months. It's a nightmare. For ten years, we've tuned our alerts to find humans. We look for those tiny delays in typing or the specific rhythm of someone moving through a network. We look for state-sponsored teams working 9-to-5 hours in another time zone. But an AI agent doesn't have a sleep cycle. It doesn't get tired. It can scout and jump across a network with a steady consistency that looks like normal system noise until the damage is done.

The claim is that this agent acted as a middleman. It might have automated the theft of data or searched for targets without needing a human to keep a constant heartbeat connection. If that's true, it changes how persistence works. An attacker doesn't have to keep a shell open anymore, and they just drop in an agent with a goal and let it loose.

You might think AI agents are just fancy scripts. We've been fighting automated scripts since the internet started. But there is a big difference here: reasoning. A script follows a pre-set tree. An agent interprets a goal and changes its path based on the mistakes it makes. Why does that matter? Because it can try ten different ways to get into a folder in seconds. It learns from every failure without tripping "too many failed attempts" alarms because it isn't slow or clumsy like a person.

This creates a second-order effect for every federal agency using outsourced services. If an agent can hide in a contractor's privileged tunnel for 60 days, the perimeter is irrelevant. It isn't just porous. The vulnerability isn't actually in the code. It's in the trust between the government and the firms they pay to keep things running.

I'll believe the denial once I see the audit logs. Until then, if you run autonomous agents, just assume you've given an attacker a force multiplier that never needs sleep.

Then there is the Polymarket situation. This one is cleaner and more predictable, which almost makes it worse, and attackers took $2.7 million from traders by hijacking a third-party script from DebugBear.

It is a classic supply chain hit. Why break into the vault when you can just compromise the guy who sells the locks? The attackers didn't go after Polymarket's core systems; they went for a monitoring tool that Polymarket trusted enough to run in the browser. Once that DebugBear script was hit, it became a vehicle for a drainer.

This is why vendor severity ratings often fail us. A vendor might call a third-party script compromise "Medium" or "High" because their own main server is fine; from a responder's view, that's a total failure. The moment an external JS file is changed to steal private keys, the CVSS score doesn't matter. You are bleeding.

The pattern here is old, and we saw this with Magecart years ago when they injected malicious code into payment gateways. But the target has shifted. We aren't just losing credit card numbers now, and we're losing direct access to crypto wallets where there isn't a "chargeback" button. Once that money moves, it's gone.

Speaking of things that are gone, law enforcement has finally brought charges in the AT&T and Ticketmaster breaches. The number being thrown around is 50 billion records.

Polymarket Supply Chain Attack Drains $2.7 Million via Hijacked Third-Party Script

Polymarket lost approximately $2.7 million of its traders’ funds in a supply chain attack on October 29, 2026. The attackers never touched Polymarket’s servers. They hijacked the DNS records of DebugBear, a page-speed monitoring vendor whose script Polymarket loaded on its international platform. They then used that script to drain signed-in traders’ wallets.Polymarket’s pages the visitor’s browser to load a Real User Monitoring (RUM) script from cdn.debugbear.com/C7xcKKrjUnXK.js. The attackers compromised DebugBear’s DNS records through its domain registrar and pointed that address to their own server. Every browser following Polymarket’s instruction received a 15 KB malicious wallet drainer in place of the monitoring script.A script loaded this way runs with the same privileges as Polymarket’s own code. The drainer used that access in three steps:Read the account - It read the login and trading API credentials Polymarket stores in the browser’s local storage, including polymarket.auth.params and poly_clob_api_key_map.Find the signer - It searched React’s internal component tree for the site’s trading client and the signer that approves the account’s transactions.Move funds - Once it had the account’s own signer sign transfers and sales, the code submitted them through Polymarket’s relayer. Positions and cash went to the attacker’s address 0x3F99139F1C5854bb628c2e576Aaf638e99dFfc18.Polymarket is refunding approximately $2.7 million to 726 affected wallets. It is also paying $1.19 million to about 5,500 wallets that lost money during the trading pause or had positions taken, for a total of $3.9 million. Traders do not need to file a claim.Polymarket removed the script within the hour, cleared all caches, reset all active login sessions and paused trading until the site was clean. It referred the case to law enforcement. DebugBear told its RUM customers to remove its embed code and is investigating the DNS hijack.What organizations and traders can doKeep third-party code off sensitive pages - A performance monitoring script has no reason to run next to a wallet signer. Load it only on other pages, host it yourself or isolate it in a sandboxed iframe.Pin scripts with Subresource Integrity (SRI) - SRI lets the browser refuse a file whose contents have changed. It would have blocked the drainer.Treat Content Security Policy (CSP) as one layer - Polymarket’s CSP allowed every host the drainer contacted, because they were all hosts Polymarket already used. A CSP limits where code can connect. It does not check what a trusted host serves.Audit the signer boundary - Check what any code on a signed-in page can ask the signer to do, and require fresh user confirmation for transfers.For traders - Review your wallet activity, reject any signing request you did not expect and ignore unofficial “refund” messages. Never share a seed phrase or private key.

The registrar says all affected domains are back, but a wallet drainer campaign reportedly took approximately $138,000 from users first

John Chen

Name.com says hackers hijacked 15 customer domains, including 10 tied to Vercel. All of the affected domains have now been restored.
That is the good news. The less good news is that the hijacked addresses reportedly sent crypto users to malicious pages built to empty their wallets.

The campaign ran between October 30 and 31, 2026. It hit at least 12 decentralized finance project websites, and estimates put the on-chain losses at approximately $138,000.
How the attack worked
Think of a domain name as the address on a storefront sign. DNS is the system that tells your browser which building that sign actually points to.
If someone gets into the registrar, the company that manages those records, they can quietly swap the building. The sign looks the same. You walk in anyway.
That is roughly what happened here. Visitors typed familiar DeFi URLs and landed on lookalike pages under attacker control.
Those pages ran a tool known as the Step Drainer. It tricked users into signing transactions they did not intend to approve, which then drained their wallets.
That distinction matters. The smart contracts behind the targeted projects stayed intact and uncompromised throughout the incident.

Every targeted domain was registered through Name.com. Registry records show that ten domains were placed on ‘client hold’ status before being restored, a status that temporarily stops a domain from resolving at all.
Who confirmed what
Name.com publicly acknowledged that domains had been improperly redirected. Alongside restoring them, the registrar told customers to review their DNS settings and turn on two-factor authentication.

DeFi projects Flap and Kintsu confirmed the attacks happened at the registrar level. Security firm Blockaid did the same.
Some teams managed to limit the damage by moving their nameservers to hosting services like Vercel or Cloudflare.
Exactly how the attackers got into the registrar layer remains unknown. Investigators are still working to pin down the entry points.
Why the front end keeps being the weak spot
DeFi likes to talk about trustless systems. Code is law, contracts are immutable, and no middleman can freeze your funds.
The website you use to reach that code, though, still runs on decidedly old-school internet plumbing. Domain registrars, DNS records and account logins sit squarely in the middle.
This incident is a clean example of that gap. The contracts did their job perfectly, and users still lost money.
Security people call this a supply-chain attack. Instead of hitting the target directly, attackers compromise a shared vendor that many targets rely on.

Malicious code on the website of prediction market Polymarket sold some signed-in traders' positions and moved their funds to the hackers on October 29. The code had replaced a page-speed script that the site loaded from an outside company.

Polymarket says it is refunding about $2.7 million to 726 affected wallets. Blockchain records show crypto worth about $2.64 million reached the hackers' wallet in under an hour.

The replaced script came from DebugBear, whose real user monitoring (RUM) tool measures how fast web pages load for real visitors.

Researchers at Hudson Rock downloaded the malicious file on October 29 from the address Polymarket's site used to load the DebugBear script. They also found a change in Polymarket's site code that removed the DebugBear script.

DebugBear's DNS records were compromised through its domain registrar, the company said on X. Its early findings indicate the attack targeted one customer's website. It has seen no sign of a break-in to its own systems, though it is still looking.

Researchers at Ohey found a different server answering for DebugBear's web addresses at 18:13 UTC, when the malicious file was still online. Earlier that day, the normal script had been served from Google Cloud Storage. Each DebugBear customer loads its own copy of the script, and the file that was swapped was Polymarket's.

How the Script Took the Money

The code reuses the access a signed-in trader already has in an open Polymarket page, Hudson Rock found after reviewing the file without running it. It reads account details that Polymarket keeps in the browser, including a set of trading API keys.

Those API keys alone cannot place an order on Polymarket, because orders also need a wallet signature. Hudson Rock found no part of the code that sends the keys, a password, a seed phrase, or a private key to the server it reports to.

Instead, the code searches the page for the part of Polymarket's site that places orders, and for the signer that approves the account's transactions.

It then takes one of two paths. For accounts that sign in with their own crypto wallet, it moves the trader's positions straight to the hackers' wallet. For accounts that sign in via email, it sells positions at ever-worse prices and then moves the money out.

In both paths, the code asks the account's own signer to sign its requests and hands them to Polymarket's relayer, which submits them. Hudson Rock said a signing request alone does not prove a trader signed without seeing a prompt. The wallet provider may still ask the trader, refuse, or apply its own rules for the session.

The wallet written into the code received its first funds at 17:10 UTC and its last at 18:02 UTC, according to Ohey's blockchain trace. In that time, it collected 28.6 million POL tokens and positions from 33 wallets.

At 18:19 UTC, those 28.6 million POL were worth about $2.64 million at DefiLlama's price of $0.0922, DefiPrime calculated. The figure covers only the POL, not the positions.

The wallet sent all 28.6 million POL on to three other addresses between 18:28 and 18:38 UTC, its transaction history shows.

Polymarket's Response and Refunds

Polymarket posted its first status update about unauthorized activity in user wallets at 17:38 UTC. At 18:05 UTC, it said its exchange was in cancel-only mode, with relayer actions paused.

The company said it removed the script "within the hour." It also cleared every cache, reset all active login sessions and paused trading until the site was clean. It has referred the case to law enforcement.
